tasks.extracted: At follow-up 62 of the 81 analysed (77%) reported using at least one of the strips provided, a median of 3 strips (IQR 1–6); 10 participants (12%) used all ten; 58% gave strips to others (denominator not stated). Strip use and results were self-reported and not verified, and reasons for not using strips (23%) were not asked. Editors' calculation: 62 of 81 is 76.5% (Wilson 95% CI 66.2–84.4%); counting all 93 given strips, 62 of 93 is 66.7% (56.6–75.4%).

Four days at a 25,000-capacity festival in England in July 2016: chemists in an on-site laboratory analysed 247 submitted substances (FTIR, colour reagent tests, mass-loss analysis); results were given in 230 brief consultations with healthcare staff lasting about 15 to 20 minutes, with harm-reduction advice and an offer to hand over further substances for police destruction.

tasks.locator: Results › Individual behavioural outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Table 3
tasks.extracted: Stated intentions from an open-ended question coded afterwards (one per client): take my usual amount 121 of 230, including 111 of 164 (67.7%) with a matching result and 4 of 45 (8.9%) with a non-matching one; throw it away myself 6 (2.6%); take it later or over a longer time 22; take a smaller amount 7; no answer 19 (8.3%). The author notes that some festival-goers may keep their other supplies in their tent and discard unwanted drugs in any nearby bin.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Model results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3)
tasks.extracted: Adjusted odds ratios for past-30-day strip use, full sample (541 people) and complete cases (212): witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months 2.444 (95% CI 1.784–3.347) and 2.257 (1.529–3.334); past-30-day heroin use 1.615 (1.107–2.357) and 1.891 (1.178–3.036); married or living as married 1.521 (1.084–2.134) and 1.608 (1.073–2.410); currently unhoused 0.679 (0.504–0.913) and 0.611 (0.410–0.909); own overdose in the past 6 months 0.981 (0.676–1.424) and 0.712 (0.416–1.218); past-30-day fentanyl use 1.332 (0.948–1.872) and 1.357 (0.879–2.095).

The 62 who used a strip and the 19 who did not differed clearly only in ever having dealt drugs (52 of 62, 84%, against 11 of 19, 58%; p = .038); ever injecting was 29 of 62 (47%) against 13 of 19 (68%; p = .099). Among those who used a strip, those with a positive result (31) against those without (31) more often used heroin weekly (20, 65%, against 3, 10%), had ever injected (25, 81%, against 8, 26%) and had ever witnessed an overdose (29, 94%, against 9, 29%) (each p < .001).

To limit the risk from false negatives, participants were told that fentanyl or its analogues may be present despite a negative strip and were instructed to practise overdose prevention whatever the result. Of the 31 with a positive result, 45% used smaller amounts, 42% went slower and 39% used with someone else around (self-report). Editors' observation: what participants did after a negative result is not reported.

tasks.locator: Results › Individual behavioural outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 105); Pilot limitations and future directions, 3rd paragraph (p. 106)
tasks.extracted: 30 of 45 clients (66.7%) whose sample did not match what it was sold as handed over further substances for police destruction, observed by the service. Possible unintended consequences, such as displacement to other drugs including alcohol (raised anecdotally by some clients after their results), were not monitored; the author argues that, as clients had already acquired the substances they submitted, testing is more likely to deter than to stimulate drug use at the festival (an argument, not a measurement).

tasks.locator: Results › Primary Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (the 2nd begins on p. 244); Table 2 (p. 245); Table 3 Panels A and B (p. 248)
tasks.extracted: Two-way fixed effects with the Borusyak et al. imputation estimator, log drug-overdose (drug-induced) deaths per 100,000 residents per state-month: test-strip coefficient without controls −0.069 (SE 0.028; p < .05) for the whole population, −0.075 (0.030) all races pooled, −0.077 (0.032) White and −0.127 (0.028; p < .01) Black, which the text gives as reductions of 6.67%, 7.22%, 7.41% and 11.92%; with age, rurality and income controls −0.074 (0.020), −0.078 (0.021), −0.083 (0.023) and −0.088 (0.026), all p < .01; 2,613, 4,181, 2,461 and 1,469 observations. Table 2: mean deaths per 100,000 residents per state-month 3.03 (SD 1.12) with a law and 2.37 (1.12) without. Editors' calculation (100(e^β − 1), 95% CI from β ± 1.96 SE): whole population −6.7% (−11.7% to −1.4%) and −7.1% (−10.7% to −3.4%); White −8.0% and Black −8.4% with controls; applied to 3.03, about 0.22 fewer deaths per 100,000 per month, 2.6 to 2.8 a year.

tasks.locator: Corrigendum p. 299, Changes 1 to 3; pp. 299–300, Change 4; p. 300, Changes 6 and 7 and closing paragraph
tasks.extracted: Corrigendum (2026; doi 10.1177/10775587261457313): the original Methods said Table 1 gave the dates when state legislatures passed statutes legalizing strips, from the Network for Public Health Law (2024); the corrected text says the authors modified some of those dates to represent the policy shock, gives implementation dates and documents the modifications in a new Online Appendix A on the coding of strip legalization. It deletes the Introduction's statements that as of 2024, 21 states and the District of Columbia had legalized strips and that the remaining states treat them as illegal paraphernalia. The journal editor states that the revisions do not alter the results or conclusions.

tasks.locator: Abstract; New Contributions (p. 241); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 246); Conclusion (p. 248)
tasks.extracted: The abstract reports a 7% decrease for the whole population and a 13.5% reduction among Black individuals, which New Contributions calls nearly twice the White reduction and the Discussion repeats; the Conclusion describes reductions in opioid overdose deaths, particularly among Black populations. Editors' calculation: 13.5% equals 100(e^0.127 − 1), the unadjusted Black coefficient with its sign reversed; correctly converted it is 11.9% (11.92% in the Results), and 8.4% with controls; no opioid-specific outcome was analysed.
tasks.quote: robust evidence that legalizing FTS is associated with significant reductions in opioid overdose deaths
